title: Peter's first sermon (Acts 2:14–36)
hook: the denier stands up and preaches, quoting Joel and the Psalms
tomorrow: the crowd asks 'what shall we do?' so what did they actually do?

segments.voice: Yesterday the news arrived each in his own language, and some in the crowd laughed it off as new wine. Someone has to answer them.
screen: `EACH IN HIS OWN LANGUAGE.` → `SOMEONE HAS TO ANSWER.`

segments.voice: After a public mistake, the hardest moment is often the next time you have to speak. Not long ago on this path, Peter stood by a fire in a courtyard and said, "I do not know the man." Now, with a crowd from every nation watching, "Peter, standing up with the eleven, lifted up his voice." He doesn't open with an apology. He answers the mockers, then reaches for a prophet: "But this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel."
screen: `THE NEXT TIME YOU SPEAK.` → `I DO NOT KNOW THE MAN.` → `PETER LIFTED UP HIS VOICE.`

segments.voice: Today's question: who does God speak through? Peter's answer is Joel's: "I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh: and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams." Then, "on my servants and on my handmaidens." Listen to that list. Daughters. Servants. The old and the young. Not only leaders, and not only people with a clean record; the man reading it aloud is proof of that. Peter goes on to a psalm of David and to what he has seen: "This Jesus hath God raised up, whereof we all are witnesses." And where the sermon lands, the promise widens again: "For the promise is unto you, and to your children, and to all that are afar off." Now something Christians share with a neighbor. Joel's words aren't only in Acts. They stand in the Jewish Bible, in the book of Joel, where the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation reads, "I will pour out My spirit upon all flesh." The same promise, all flesh, sons and daughters, old and young, stands in both Bibles. And one honest difference: Peter reads Joel as coming true that morning, through Jesus. Jewish tradition reads Joel within Israel's own story, and not through Peter's reading of Jesus. One set of words, held by two peoples, read two ways. One to tell a friend: Joel says afterward; Peter says in the last days.
screen: `WHO DOES GOD SPEAK THROUGH?` · `ALL FLESH: DAUGHTERS, SERVANTS, OLD.` · `UNTO YOU, AND TO YOUR CHILDREN.` · `JOEL, IN THE JEWISH BIBLE TOO.` · then, large: `THE PROMISE IS FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: Write by hand the first sentence you'd say if you had to speak again after a stumble: to a friend, a class, a team. Keep it short and true, with no apology speech attached. If you pray, you can offer it up; if not, read it once, slowly, and let it stand.
Peter's first sermon. The man who denied Jesus stands up, reads Joel's promise to all flesh, and tells what he has seen.
Your line: the promise is for you, and for your children, and for the ones far off. See you tomorrow.

notes: Unity thread (wisdom day): the shared thing is Joel's promise itself, quoted from JPS 1917 (Joel 3:1 in Jewish numbering): 'I will pour out My spirit upon all flesh'. Confirm the JPS wording exactly. The honest difference: Peter reads Joel as fulfilled that morning through Jesus; Jewish tradition reads Joel within Israel's own story. Ranking neither; a Jewish reviewer should confirm it reads fairly.
'Stands in both Bibles': Joel is in the Jewish Bible and the Christian Old Testament; no claim is made about public reading. Confirm.
'Joel says afterward; Peter says in the last days': KJV Joel 2:28 and JPS Joel 3:1 both say 'afterward'; Acts 2:17 says 'in the last days'. Confirm.
Acts 2:23 and 2:36 ('ye have crucified') are left out on purpose; they need careful framing (Rome executed Jesus) and a short lesson can't give it.
Acts 2:39 (tomorrow's reading range) is quoted here because the carry comes from it; 1491 focuses on 2:42–47.
'Not long ago on this path' points back to day 1480 (Matthew 26:69–75); 'I do not know the man' is Matthew 26:72.
